instructions: Rewrite `callout.text` per beat: 2-4 words, concrete and loaded, in the viewer's second person where it fits.
NEVER an abstract noun (ORGANIZATION / MANAGEMENT / INFORMATION). Prefer what a person can see, feel or do.
Set callout to null when the beat has no hook worth stamping — silence is a valid, good choice.
`style`: reveal (3-4 words) | highlight (2 words) | strike (a negation) | outline (a real stat) | box | stack.
`concept`: the beat's LITERAL subject → a scene icon that gets shown instead of talking heads.

Allowed: alarmClock, butterfly, subway, car, coffee, codeWindow, rocketLaunch, funnelMetrics, dollarExchange, laptopMockup, crash, ledge, water, grave, medical, notes, phone, school, home, family, road, storm, star, heart, fire, tree, mask, mirror, key, law, photo, war, game, work, city, food, coin, door, lightbulb, shadowSelf, puppeteer, chains, compass, dominoCascade, icebergDepth, funnelTrap, thirtyTyrants, ringOfGyges, caveAllegory, shipOfState, tripartiteSoul, kallipolis, fiveRegimes, mythOfEr, boulder, summit, ladder, crack, clock, balance, book, shield, trophy, hourglass, sword, target, magnifier, wallet, gift, inheritance, zap. Set a string when the beat is really ABOUT that thing
(a crash, a home, a lake, a wall of notes); null or omitted = no icon (there is no lexicon
fallback). Use only when it's the true subject — a wrong icon is worse than none. The icon must
be in the book's story-bible visualProvenance.allowedMotifs or it is dropped with a warning.
`set` (optional): the location, one of the renderer's sets — honoured as written.
`shotOverride` (optional): force a framing. `shot` above is only the director's first guess.
The director stages the body itself from the concept — a beat whose subject is a
letter/phone/key/photo/book/coin/mirror/mask/idea/compass/meal/love/job/court puts that
object IN THE LEAD'S HAND, an outdoor beat can make them walk across the set, an indoor
one can sit them down. You do not author that here; naming the right `concept` is what
turns it on. A wrong concept costs more now than it used to.
`diagram`: an EXPLANATORY self-drawing graphic that BECOMES the whole beat (cast dropped,
no callout). Author one ONLY on a genuinely conceptual beat; leave null otherwise — a weak
or generic diagram is worse than none. Use at most a handful across the whole book. Shape:
{ type, title?, labels[], values[] }, where type is one of:
sorter   — a taxonomy sorting into buckets. labels = the 2-4 category names; values = optional per-bucket counts.
matchWave— two rhythms drifting then locking into sync. labels[0] = the payoff word (e.g. IN SYNC).
flow     — a cause→effect chain. labels = 2-3 ordered node names.
spectrum — a marker on a continuum. labels = [leftPole, rightPole]; values = [0..1 marker position].
Keep labels 1-2 words. Best on the beat that first NAMES a framework, a sync, a process or a scale.

`concept: null` means NO icon on this beat (not even a decorative one); omitting the key is ALSO no icon — there is no lexicon fallback (Faz 0). Every beat needs an entry; an unauthored beat fails gate-authorship.
Do not leave a beat silent when its narration names concrete things (a list of objects, an anecdote, a person doing something) — give it the narrator's phrase or the object.
Prefer the narrator's concrete phrase over an abstract metaphor label ("PAUSE THE IMPULSE", not "A LOGIC FILTER").
A diagram title must not promise a shape its type cannot draw (no "LOOP"/"PYRAMID" on a straight flow).
Keep the array order and length. Then re-run plan-antidote with --callouts=<this file>.
After re-running: node scripts/audit-antidote.js --slug=<slug> — it FAILS the plan if any
window runs longer than 8s with nothing happening on screen.

Diem conversely draws her literal physical magical strength directly from her bond to her people and to Luther. She weaponizes the very connections Oas
is trying to destroy, using that communal strength to push back the Hearthstone's influence, which brings Diem to the absolute climax of her character arc and the ultimate test of the bond.
We find Diem standing entirely alone before they ever flame. It is this hauntingly beautiful scene.
There are rivers of pure light pulsing up the ancient bark of the tree. And sitting casually by the roots
is this mysterious red-haired man. An old god. An old god completely forgotten by the modern world of Emarion.
He is just tossing a single glowing ember in his palm and he's singing this deeply unsettling
chilling tune. Life for life. Life for life. This is the cosmic accounting of the Immarian universe.
The magic requires balance. The hardest battle Diem faces in this entire series
isn't actually defeating Ofuca or commanding armies. No, it is the deeply personal decision of whether to accept a beautiful, well-earned piece or to willingly choose to return to the
immense suffering, messiness, and pain of the living world. And it is so crucial that she actually sees what that peace looks like.
It isn't an abstract concept. She watches Ignas, who has been trapped in purgatory for millennia, finally break the curse.
Ignos lets out this choked, sobbing cry and launches herself into the arms of a tall, copper- skinned man with dark braids, her long lost mortal mate.
After thousands of years of agonizing waiting, the Kindred are finally allowed to cross over into the afterlife to be with the ones they love.
The peace is real. It is palpable. And it is right there waiting for Diem. And honestly, no, she deserves it.
Oh, absolutely. Diem has been tortured, manipulated, and beaten down. She saved the world. She freed the ancient kindred.
She stopped the shadow god. She has paid her dues 10 times over. She has earned the right to walk into that fire and finally rest.
And she even sees her brother Teller, calling out to her from the other side. Her family is waiting. She has done enough.
Let her rest. I felt the exact same way reading it. I was practically yelling at the book, "Just go. Be at peace." Right?
But then the red-haired old god does something very specific and deeply cruel. He doesn't argue with her.
He just shows her an image of the mortal And in that image, she sees Luther. He is suddenly clutching his chest, freezing midstep,
his face contorted in It's the cosmic trap. Exactly. Because of the bond.
If Diem takes her well-deserved rest and walks into the afterlife, she is completely abandoning the tether that kept her fighting in the first place.
Her peace, her beautiful rest with her brother would trigger Luther's absolute agonizing destruction.
And there is the thesis fully realized. She cannot choose the sweet, quiet release of the afterlife because her bond to Luther literally, physically
tethers her soul to the living world. The bond is her gravity. It is the only thing powerful enough to pull her back from the edge of heaven itself.
So after exploring all of this, the history, the magic, the psychological torture, we have to take an honest step back and view this from a highly critical almost cynical perspective.
Let's do it. We have exhaustively established that this intense, unavoidable, magical bond drives every single major decision these two characters make.
But does this bond actually make Diem and Luther really terrible leaders? It is a totally
valid necessary question to ask of a fantasy series. Right? Because if I am a mundane soldier in the Amaran army, sitting in the freezing mud,
starving, waiting for the shadow gods army to attack, shouldn't I be completely terrified that my two top commanders are making massive realmaltering
military decisions based entirely on their magical, romantic obsession with each other? The evidence for that fear is incredibly damning.

We skipped over a moment earlier that perfectly illustrates this. Let's go back to Luther and the flame root bomb. Arrow tells Luther that Teller has successfully created a flame root bomb that could potentially
neutralize Ophus' mind control magic. This bomb could theoretically save thousands upon thousands of lives on the All Arly needs
is to make a tiny superficial cut on Luther's hand to test if the bomb actually works against descended magic. And what does Luther do?
The seasoned general, the man who has fought for survival his entire life. He outright refuses. He violently snaps at her and says, "Absolutely not." And his reasoning
is baffling from a military perspective. He refuses to risk even a paper cut. He refuses to risk even a temporary 5-minute loss of his magic because he cannot tolerate even a
fraction of a chance that he might be incapacitated when Diem finally escapes Cordial and needs him. It is breathtakingly reckless.
He is actively prioritizing his own physical ability to protect one woman over testing a weapon that could literally save the entire continent from genocide.
When you look at that, you have to ask, does this intense, consuming romance actually undercut the political and military stakes of the entire book?
Are they objectively terrible generals because they prioritize their love over the realm they are supposed to be
It's the most fair critique a reader could make. It makes them flawed, unpredictable, and yes, objectively
reckless generals. but, and this is where I think Penol's writing elevates the entire genre. If we synthesize everything we've just unpacked today about Amarian's history, yes, the bond
makes them flawed. But that exact same flaw is the only thing that makes them capable of finally breaking the violent millennialong cycle of Aaran's
history. Expand on that because that is the crucial reframing of the whole narrative.
Think about the original Kindred. How did they destroy the world? They destroyed the world because they tried to legally,
magically, and systematically control their grief and their bonds. They built toxic stone temples to manage mortal perception.

They used Umbra's magic to wipe memories to avoid the pain of their mistakes. They created draconian progyny laws to control love and bloodlines. They tried to clinicalize and control the bond, and it resulted in a world of endless
war and oppression. and Diem and Diem and Luther save the world by doing the exact opposite. They don't try to neatly manage or hide from the agonizing messy reality of their bond.
They let their bond burn the old corrupt system down to the ground. They weaponize their So, the bond isn't a distraction from the war.
No. For Crown of Amarion, the bond is the war. Which leaves us with one final deeply unsettling question to turn over in our minds as we close the book on this deep dive.
What's that? We heard the old god at the Everflame state the cosmic law very clearly.
The magic requires a life for a life to balance the forging spell.
If Diem ultimately chooses to turn her back on heaven and return to the mortal realm for Luther,

Something to think about long after the embers burn out.
